3348.t: Traditionally derived from Proto-Indo-European *kʷelh₁- (“far (in time or space)”).

3312.t: Potentially haplologized from *μελιλίχια (*melĭlĭ́khĭă), from Proto-Indo-European *mélit (“honey”) + *leyǵʰ- (“lick”). Compare Albanian bletë and Sanskrit मधुलिह् (madhulih).

3380.t: From τρώγω (trṓgō, “to bite; to eat”), through the concept of an animal chewing a hole.

3358.t: From an unattested *στρατιάομαι (*stratiáomai) + -της (-tēs). Another analysis (ultimately from the same root) takes the word as a derivative in -ιώτης (-iṓtēs) of στρατός (stratós, “troop, department of the people”).

3393.t: From Proto-Hellenic *kʰérsos, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰérsos, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰers- (“stand erect”). Cognate to Albanian djerr (“fallow land”); Latin horreō, horror; Sanskrit हर्ष (harṣa, “excitement”).

3319.t: Probably from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ers- (“tail, butt”) (alternatively reconstructed as Proto-Indo-European *h₃érsos (“backside, buttocks”)), and related to ὄρρος (órrhos, “butt, ass”); see there for more.

3309.t: From Proto-Indo-European *mus- (“a fly”), whence also Latin musca, Old Church Slavonic моуха (muxa), Old Armenian մուն (mun), Albanian mizë, Latvian muša, Old English mycg (English midge).

3373.t: From συνίστημι (sŭnĭ́stēmĭ, “to place together, associate, unite”) + -μα (-mă).

3377.t: From Proto-Hellenic *tʰrākʰús (whence Mycenaean Greek 𐀲𐀨𐀐𐀹(𐀊) (ta-ra-ke-wi(ja))), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰréh₂gʰ-us ~ *dʰr̥h₂gʰ-éws (“rough”), from *dʰreh₂gʰ- (“to irritate”). Compare θράσσω (thrā́ssō).

3394.t: From Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰutrom, from *ǵʰew- (“to pour”), whence χέω (khéō, “to pour out”); the original meaning was perhaps a "container of liquids (poured things)". Cognate with Sanskrit होत्र (hotrá).

3308.t: Origin uncertain. It may be related to either Proto-Indo-European *mew- (“damp”) (as in 'flowing' like the countless waves of the sea) or μύρμηξ (múrmēx, “ant”) (like a countless swarm).

3350.t: From Proto-Indo-European *pōlH-o-s, from *pelH- (“young animal”). Compare Latin pullus.

3397.t: From ἀθάνατος (āthắnătos, “undying”) + -ία (-ĭ́ā, abstract noun suffix). The τ (t) changed to σ (s) by palatalization.

3386.t: Traditionally derived from Proto-Indo-European *bʰendʰ- (“to tie”), the same root of Sanskrit बन्ध॑ति (bándhati) and Proto-Germanic *bindaną. The same suffix is recognized in Gaulish benna and Welsh ben (“cart”).

3370.t: Clearly related to σφεδανός (sphedanós, “violent, vehement”). The origin of these words is uncertain but perhaps related to σφαδᾴζω (sphadāízō, “to flounce”) and σφενδόνη (sphendónē, “sling”).

3347.t: Possibly from Proto-Indo-European *puḱ- (“press together”); compare Avestan 𐬞𐬎𐬯𐬁 (pusā, “headband, diadem”), as well as Albanian putë.

3384.t: According to Beekes, from the same Pre-Greek root of φρίξ (phríx, “shivering”).

3351.t: Has been connected with Ancient Greek σάττω (sáttō, “to stuff, to press”), but this is semantically insufficient.

3313.t: From Proto-Hellenic *mérimnā, probably from Proto-Indo-European *(s)mer- (“to remember”). Cognate with μέρμερος (mérmeros, “anxious”), Old English ġemimor (“mindful, remembering”) and Latin memor (“mindful”).

3315.t: According to Beekes, probably of Pre-Greek origin.

3320.t: Has often been connected with πλάσσω (plássō, “to knead”), παλάμη (palámē, “flat of the hand”) and πέλανος (pélanos, “dough, pulp”). However, the semantics of this etymology are not compelling.

3318.t: From an archaic form *ϝουλή (*woulḗ), from Proto-Indo-European *welh₃- (“to hit”). Closest cognates are Latin vulnus (“wound”) and Irish fuil (“blood”).

3369.t: From συν- (sun-, “with, together”) + στέλλω (stéllō, “to dispatch, to send”).

3372.t: Probably from Σάρδεις (Sắrdeis, “Sardis”) + -ιον (-ĭon, diminutive suffix), because it was its place of origin.

3346.t: Of disputed origin: * According to an extensive discussion by Hackstein, Tocharian B pyāk-tsi (“to strike down”) is related, which requires a reconstruction of the common root as Proto-Indo-European *pyeh₂(k)- (“to strike down”) (rather than as *pteh₂-k-).

3352.t: Iterative-intensive formation in -τάω (-táō) from σκαίρω (skaírō, “to skip, dance”), which is probably from Proto-Indo-European *sker- (“to jump”).

3354.t: From the o-stem variant of σκότος (skótos, “darkness”) + -όω (-óō).
